properties.name: Golden Gate Crossing · Borrowed Launches
properties.summary: With no boat of its own at San Francisco, the government borrowed launches from the San Blas ships then in port to ferry the horses across the mouth of the harbour, so that Goycoechea could ride north to open a road to Bodega. Savage's entry for the governor's despatch gives 34 horses crossed; Bancroft, summarising the same business, says some thirty. Goycoechea set out on 5 August 1793 with a sergeant and ten men. The same entry carries the governor's judgement on the overland route: «el grande rodeo y tierra incognita».
properties.result: Spain borrows boats from visiting ships to cross its own harbour mouth

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 14), tomo xxii, orig. p. ~290 / scan n112, Doc 99. The Bodega land expedition.
Bancroft, History of California I, 507.

properties.name: Goycoechea's Overland Expedition to Bodega
properties.summary: 10 soldiers + sergeant march overland from SF via Bolinas and Tomales Bay to Bodega. Coast Miwok direct them to harder western route; later admitted "deceived." Territory 45 miles north of SF is "tierra incognita."
properties.result: "Tierra incognita"; Spain's own governor admits unknown territory

properties.name: Moraga's 1806 Interior Expedition
properties.summary: The first long reconnaissance of the Central Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, with Fr. Pedro Munoz as chaplain and diarist. The rivers the party named on the way north were the Merced, the Dolores, the Guadalupe and the San Francisco, a dry bed; the large river they reached on 4 October already carried the name Rio de la Pasion from an earlier expedition looking for a land route to Bodega. Bancroft doubts they got as far as the Sacramento at all, finding nothing in the narrative to suggest the Pasion was so large a river, and reads the sequence instead as the Tuolumne, the Stanislaus and the Calaveras. Reconnaissance only; nothing was occupied.
properties.result: A round trip; no occupation, and the northern limit unsettled

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 52-54.

Munoz's diary, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (1960), chap. III. Mapped stop by stop at maps/zalvidea-moraga-1806.html.

properties.name: Moraga's 2nd Expedition · Sacramento Valley
properties.summary: Second interior campaign. Again, a round trip.

sources.citation: Cutter 1957.

properties.name: Battle of Suisun
properties.summary: 17 men cross Carquinez Strait by boat to attack Suisun ranchería. Suisun had killed 16 Christians over prior 3 years. Hard fight; survivors in huts preferred to "perish in the flames" rather than surrender. Moraga received royal commendations.
properties.result: Spanish tactical victory at the frontier chokepoint

sources.citation: C-A 12; C-A 25; Bancroft II:91 fn.24.

Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales tocante a la Alta California, Tomo 1, ch. 10, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 151, recounting Alférez José Sánchez's narration. Vallejo's footnote records that the phrase stands in English in the original manuscript.

properties.notes: Malaca's words come from Vallejo's memoir of the 1870s reporting what Alférez Sánchez told him, not from a contemporary record, and Vallejo wrote the phrase in English. Earlier versions of this map rendered it into Spanish and presented that rendering as the source wording. Bancroft flags the provenance problem directly: Vallejo places this fight with Jose Sanchez in 1817 rather than Moraga in 1810, Alvarado dates it 1817 but puts Moraga in command, and Bancroft concludes 'It is possible that the author has confounded two different battles' (History of California II, n. 29). Malaca's words reach us only through that account.

quote.en: Chief Malaca, as Vallejo reports him: "it is better to die free than to live as slaves, despised by our Puy (priest)."
quote.source: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales tocante a la Alta California, Tomo 1, ch. 10, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 151, recounting Alférez José Sánchez's narration. Vallejo's footnote records that the phrase stands in English in the original manuscript.

properties.name: Reports of a Ship at Bodega
properties.summary: Arguello reports to Arrillaga that twenty or more otter canoes have been sighted heading for the San Jose esteros, that the Christian Indians of San Francisco say many are taking otter, and that the gentiles say a large ship is lying at Bodega. The nationality of that ship is not established in the despatch. The first inspection of Bodega the record shows is Moraga's of 1812, and his diary describes an American vessel there with Alaskan hunters aboard, not a Russian one. The map previously credited an autumn 1810 reconnaissance with forty Aleut canoes and Russian supply ships at anchor; neither is in the despatch.
properties.result: The Spanish learn of Bodega from the gentiles, and do not go

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 741-743 / Savage pp. 275-276 / scan n278-n279. Luis Arguello to Arrillaga, San Francisco, 19 September 1810.

properties.name: Moraga Discovers Fort Ross
properties.summary: Moraga with 4 soldiers investigates grounded vessel. Discovers Fort Ross: ~80 men, Kuskov commanding, all from Unalaska/Kamchatka. Vessel 8 leagues above Bodega. No opposition.
properties.result: Discovery; no confrontation possible

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1045-1048 / Savage pp. 320-322 / scan n327-n329. Luis Arguello to Arrillaga, San Francisco, 31 July 1812, on the otter hunters in the bay and the first verification mission to Bodega; leaf read.

Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1215-1217 / Savage pp. 364, 367-368 / scan n371, Doc 439. Gabriel Moraga's reconnaissance and defence assessment of the Russian post at Ross, San Francisco, 30 July 1814 (unsigned). Doc 432 in the same volume, which an earlier citation named, is Argüello's earthquake report of January 1813.
Mathes (ed.), Documentos para la historia de la Alta California: the same despatches as his Docs 10 and 11.

properties.name: Moraga's Fort Ross Defense Assessment
properties.summary: 40 Russians, 80 Aleuts, 12 guns (4-pounder), 3 falconets. Spanish troops: "no shirts, no pants, no hats." The most damning comparison in the archive.
properties.result: Russians armed and supplied; Spanish naked

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), orig. pp. 1215-17 / scan n371, Doc 439: Gabriel Moraga's reconnaissance and defence assessment of the Russian establishment at Ross, 1814.

properties.name: Argüello's Northern Expedition
properties.summary: 55 men; one of the largest Spanish/Mexican expeditions in CA history. Two full days spent ferrying horses across Carquinez Strait with 4 assembled boats. A power that needs a weekend to cross a channel does not control the territory beyond it.
properties.result: Two days to cross the Strait; not an empire moving through its own territory

sources.citation: Ordaz, Diario, 1821, MS. Bancroft II:444–446.

properties.name: Colnett's Argonaut at Bodega
properties.summary: British ship takes refuge during storm; cuts spars, makes repairs. Later misidentified by Spanish as active English threat. Ghost presence that haunted Spanish intelligence for years.

properties.name: Vancouver's 1st Visit to San Francisco
properties.summary: HMS Discovery and Chatham anchor at SF. Warm reception from Commandant Sal. Menzies walks to Fort Point; finds one cannon "lash'd to a log of Wood." British see the weakness firsthand.
properties.result: British assess SF defenses; one burst cannon

properties.name: English at Bodega "con los cañones en tierra"
properties.summary: Arrillaga reports an English vessel anchored at Bodega with "cannons on land." Identity uncertain; Colnett traces? New vessel? Rumor? Same year as Spanish Bodega failure.
properties.result: Foreign military presence in territory Spain cannot reach

properties.name: Menzies Lands at Bodega
properties.summary: Menzies landed from the Chatham with Lieutenant Puget on 20 October 1793. The ship came in through a passage half a mile wide, a steep rocky bluff to port and a small rocky island to starboard that Menzies named Gibson's Island, and anchored in six fathoms; the latitude they took by observation at the anchorage was 38 deg. 19' 30" N. On the bluff headland they found a cross lately put up, made of a piece of a cask stave lashed to a pole with a rope yarn, and the grass and brush recently burned off. Walking down to the channel they came on a hut and a party of Coast Miwok who sat down at their approach and called out 'Amico', friend, a word Menzies had no doubt they had from the Spaniards, 'as we afterwards found that they spoke many words of the language of that Nation'. A woman offered them fish from a basket, under the name Piscau. The 1924 editor glossed the inland water behind the beach as Tomales Bay, and that gloss is why this landing is often placed there; Wagner, working from Goycoechea's and Matute's accounts, puts the cross on Bodega Head, and the latitude agrees with Bodega.
properties.result: The British find the traces of a Spanish establishment that was already abandoned

sources.citation: Menzies' California journal, California Historical Society Quarterly 2, no. 4 (1924), 301-04.

Wagner, 'The Last Spanish Exploration of the Northwest Coast', CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 338: the cross on Bodega Head, and Menzies' visit to Bodega Bay dated 20 October 1793. Wagner also reads Gibson's Island as Menzies' mistake for Colnett's 1790 call.

properties.name: Vancouver's 2nd Visit · Concealment Policy
properties.summary: Dramatic change from 1st visit. Armed guards, 2-mile limit, refused access to mission. But 8 new brass 4-pounders visible on beach, workers building battery. Spain scrambles to hide weakness and show strength simultaneously.
properties.result: Concealment policy; Spain hides its defenses from the one power that matters

properties.name: The San Diego Commandant Shows the Bodega Plan
properties.summary: At San Diego in late November 1793 the commandant showed Vancouver's officers his plan of the opening six leagues north of Point Reyes where he said a settlement had been attempted that summer, and the plan carried a sketch of both waters with their Spanish names. Menzies distinguishes the commandant from Captain Zuniga throughout, and the commandant at that date was Antonio Grajera, whose predecessor Zuniga had handed over on 19 October 1793 and was waiting to leave. The plan was shown while access was being closed down: on seeing how many of the English had walked up, the commandant asked that they take their walk another way, since his orders did not allow so many into the presidio, and afterwards only officers were let that far. Bancroft reads the same visit as courteous reception hemmed in by Arrillaga's 'severe and inhospitable injunctions'. Not an absence of concealment, but a chart given away while the gate was shut.
properties.result: A chart shown and the presidio closed, in the same week

sources.citation: Menzies' California journal, CHSQ 2, no. 4 (1924), 335.

Bancroft, History of California I, 491, 666: Zuniga in command until October 1793, his successor taking the offices on the 19th; Vancouver's ships at San Diego 27 November to 9 December 1793, received by Grajera and Zuniga.

properties.name: English Launches at Santa Cruz
properties.summary: English launches spotted off Santa Cruz coast, withdrew. Sgt. Pedro Amador sent as reinforcement. Soldier Mesa punished for misreporting.
properties.result: English probe; withdrew

properties.name: English Shipwreck at Point Reyes / Farallones
properties.summary: Ship sinks near Farallones. Indigenous informants report two uniformed Englishmen at Point Reyes. English naval presence at the Bay entrance during wartime. The report comes through indigenous intelligence networks.
properties.result: English at the Bay entrance; indigenous networks provide the warning

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 8), tomo xiv, orig. pp. 371-373 / Savage p. 313 / leaf 116 / scan n312. Caro de Alterni to Borica, San Francisco, 14 April 1797, «Naufragio de un buque desconocido»: a body washed up near Punta de Reyes; P. Landaeta's mayordomo reported a ship seen between the Farallones that shortly disappeared; the gentiles said they had seen two uniformed men who were English.

properties.name: English Vessel at Santa Cruz
properties.summary: English ship arrives at Santa Cruz port, 60 miles from SF Bay. Vallejo coordinates with alcalde; no military officer available. Thin defense exposed.
properties.result: No military response possible

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 8), tomo xv, orig. pp. 501-502 / Savage p. 351 / leaf 155 / scan n350. Vallejo to Borica, San Jose, 1 October 1797, «Sobre un buque Ingles llegado a Santa Cruz»: an English vessel at the port of Santa Cruz; Vallejo arranged assistance with the alcalde, there being no war officer present, and reported himself ready if called.

properties.name: English Corsair Campaign · Gulf of California
properties.summary: 4 English frigates (22–24 guns each) raided Gulf of California shipping. Ransomed ships, captured brigs. Governor Arrillaga: "sin ningunos elementos de defensa." Maritime reinforcement route to California contested.
properties.result: English naval dominance; supply route threatened

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 14), tomo xxi, orig. pp. 65-93 / Savage pp. 16-30: Arrillaga's dispatches on the English corsair crisis, 1799.

properties.name: HMS Raccoon at San Francisco
properties.summary: British warship from Columbia River. HMS Raccoon had seized Fort Astoria Dec 1813. Needed gunpowder. Crew deserting to Spanish protection as "Roman Catholics." Written in English in the archive.
properties.result: British warship uses SF as supply port; War of 1812 reaches Pacific

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1240-1244 / scan n380. Capt. Black of HMS Raccoon to the Governor, March 1814, written in English: the ship grounded on the bar leaving the Columbia and 'made much water which ruined her powder'; he asks for 1,400 to 1,500 lbs of gunpowder, and reports that some of his crew 'intend to desert & claim the protection of the Spanish Authorities under plea of being Roman Catholics'.

properties.name: Eliza's Activa at Bodega: Spain's Last Pacific Exploration
properties.summary: Francisco de Eliza's call at Bodega on the way south, on the last exploring expedition Spain sent up this coast. He had left San Blas on 30 April 1793 with the schooner Mexicana under Martinez y Zayas, and got no higher than about 44 degrees before settled winds and a want of water turned him back; only the schooner reached the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Eliza stopped at Trinidad for wood and water, then at Bodega, examining the coast between them, as Wagner says, superficially, and went on to San Francisco, where he sent his pilots to chart the bay, and then down to Monterey and San Diego. Wagner's verdict on him is flat: distinctly, he was a failure. The empire's reach was not starving but it had stopped going north.
properties.result: Spain's last northwest exploration turns back at 44 degrees

sources.citation: Wagner, 'The Last Spanish Exploration of the Northwest Coast', CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 318-19.
Bancroft, History of California I, 509 n.50, for the Activa's arrival at San Francisco on 11 August 1793.

properties.name: Rezanov Arrives on Juno
properties.summary: Nikolai Rezanov; Imperial Chamberlain, RAC shareholder, diplomat. Arrives at SF. Concepción Argüello courtship. Intelligence gathering on Spanish defenses. First Russian official at SF.
properties.result: Russia assesses Spanish California firsthand

sources.citation: Bancroft II; Gibson & Istomin 2014.

properties.name: RAC Fur-Collecting Begins at Bodega
properties.summary: 130 Aleut hunters aboard Kodiak. First Russian representative: Tarakanov. 40+ Russians + 150 Indians by 1809 (Argüello report). Moraga protests; ignored.
properties.result: Permanent Russian presence established; Spain protests but cannot act

sources.citation: Milliken 2009:22–25; C-A 12.

properties.name: Fifty Bidarkas in the Bay, 130 Reported on the Coast
properties.summary: Luis Arguello reports fifty bidarkas counted inside San Francisco Bay, and 130 reported to him between Point Bonita and San Antonio; the hunters' canoes between them held more men than the whole mission. Six neophytes out hunting seals for their padres were briefly held by the hunters as suspected spies and then let go. No ship was seen. The coast figure is what the Indians told him, not what the Spanish counted.
properties.result: Russian hunting inside the bay, in numbers the presidio could not match

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 983-986 / Savage pp. 306-307 / scan n311-n313. Luis Arguello to Arrillaga, San Francisco, 30 May 1811.

properties.name: Farallon Islands · Russian Sealing Station
properties.summary: The Russian-American Company's sealing station on the Farallones, about 29 miles west of the Golden Gate by the coordinates plotted here. Aleut hunters camped there through the season, taking seals, sea lions and birds' eggs for Ross. Neither Spain nor Mexico ever contested the occupation.
properties.result: Russian territory visible from SF; unchallenged

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 296-98, 631-32.

properties.name: Kotzebue Visits on Rurik
properties.summary: Otto von Kotzebue arrives at SF on scientific circumnavigation. Spain demands Ross abandonment. Diplomatic failure; Russia ignores the demand.
properties.result: Spanish diplomatic protest; Russia ignores it

sources.citation: James R. Gibson and Alexei A. Istomin (eds.), Russian California, 1806-1860: A History in Documents (Hakluyt Society), Doc. 32.

properties.name: Golovnin on Kamchatka at SF
properties.summary: Captain Golovnin arrives at SF on world circumnavigation aboard Kamchatka. Same season as Russian Kutuzov and American Ontario. Three-power naval convergence in one month.
properties.result: Three-power convergence: Russia + Russia + America in SF at once

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. p. 197 / Savage p. 446 / leaf 450, entry of 5 October 1818: «Da parte de arribada de fragata expedicionaria Rusa Kamtschatca», orig. pp. 626-627. Partly cited by Bancroft.
Golovnin, Around the World on the Kamchatka, 1817-1819, trans. Ella Lury Wiswell (Honolulu: Hawaiian Historical Society, 1979).

properties.name: Russian Kutuzov at SF
properties.summary: RAC vessel Kutuzov at SF alongside Golovnin's warship and American Ontario. Spanish garrison watches foreign warships parade through their port.

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. p. 197 / Savage p. 446 / leaf 450, entry of 2 September 1818: «arribada de fragata Rusa 'Cotknoff' [Kutuzov], Corbeta Americana de guerra Ontario», orig. pp. 624-625. Partly cited by Bancroft.

properties.name: Vasiliev's Corvettes at San Francisco
properties.summary: Luis Arguello reports to Governor Sola the arrival of the Russian war corvettes Otkrytie and Blagonamerennyi, anchored on the 22nd at three in the afternoon, and says he will receive them cordially and hospitably, as his standing orders required. They had sailed past a fort that by its own commander's account four months earlier had six serviceable guns.
properties.result: Russian warships pass an unserviceable fort and are received as guests

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. i.1146-1147 / Savage p. 276 / scan n275, Doc 366. Luis Arguello to Gov. Sola, San Francisco, 23 November 1820.

properties.name: Hagemeister Treaty with Kashaya Pomo
properties.summary: Russia negotiates land cession with Kashaya Pomo chiefs; not Spanish authorities. "Allies of Russia" medals distributed 1819. Russians treat indigenous peoples as sovereign landowners because, north of the Bay, they are.
properties.result: Russia treats Pomo as sovereign; Spain does not exist here

sources.citation: Protocol of the meeting at Colony Ross between the Indian tribal chiefs and Captain-Lieutenant Hagemeister, 22 September 1817. Archives of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire, published by the Fort Ross Conservancy Digital Library in the 2012 bicentennial collection of sixteen documents.

properties.name: Battle of Punta de Guijarros · Lelia Byrd
properties.summary: First naval engagement between a Spanish battery and foreign vessel. American smuggling + armed rescue + artillery duel. Shaler's crew put pistols to Spanish guards' chests. Ship escaped under grapeshot fire. Spanish soldiers were complicit in the otter skin trade.
properties.result: First foreign attack on California; American smugglers

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), orig. pp. 633-636 (leaves 256-262): Rodriguez to Arrillaga, 10 April 1803, on the affair at Punta de los Guijarros; with the Lelia Byrd's Norfolk dispatch of 1 April 1801 at orig. pp. 641-642, Vidalva's petition for 233 otter skins at 645-647, and Velasquez's defence of 11 April 1803 at 648-650. None of these is cited by Bancroft.
Shaler, Journal of a Voyage Between China and the North-Western Coast of America (1808); Cleveland, A Narrative of Voyages and Commercial Enterprises (1842), for the two American accounts.

properties.name: American Frigate at SF · Troop Crisis
properties.summary: Damaged American frigate anchors in SF port. Argüello forced to pull invalidos (retired soldiers) from San José to augment escorts. Chronic troop shortage: presidio can't staff itself when a foreign ship appears.
properties.result: One foreign ship exposes garrison collapse

sources.citation: Pueblo Papers (Bancroft Library), PP 0389.

properties.name: USS Ontario at San Francisco
properties.summary: American warship Ontario at SF; same month as Golovnin's Kamchatka and RAC Kutuzov. Three nations' vessels in the Bay simultaneously. Spain watches.
properties.result: American warship in the Bay

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. p. 197 / Savage p. 446 / leaf 450, entry of 2 September 1818, which reports the Russian frigate and the American corvette Ontario at San Francisco together, orig. pp. 624-625. Partly cited by Bancroft.

properties.name: Mercury Trial · Capt. Eyres
properties.summary: Boston captain, 8 years trading with Russians and NW Coast Indians. Testimony at Santa Barbara. American commercial penetration of the coast; trading network connecting Boston, Russian Alaska, and California.
properties.result: American-Russian commercial network exposed

sources.citation: C-A 12, scan n360.

properties.name: The Brig Cosak at Guaymas
properties.summary: Antonio Cordero reports to Governor Sola from Arispe: the brig Cosak tried to water at Guaymas, was threatened with sinking for having no port captain aboard and its captain jailed, then got under way, raised the Anglo-American flag, fired three cannon shots and fled with abuse. Cordero orders it seized wherever it arrives, anyone who lands arrested and the goods confiscated. The same winter as Bouchard, on the other shore of the gulf.
properties.result: Anglo-American defiance in the Gulf in the same season as Bouchard

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. i.1001-1004 / Savage p. 221 / scan n220, Doc 277. Antonio Cordero to Gov. Sola, Arispe, 7 January 1818.

properties.name: Bouchard's Attack on Monterey
properties.summary: Hipolito Bouchard, sailing under Buenos Aires colours, took Monterey with the Argentina of thirty-eight guns and the Santa Rosa of twenty-six. The prisoners put his crews at about 285, a figure Bancroft thinks probably exaggerated; Sola reported 400 men landed. The presidio and the castillo were burned. Sola fell back on the Salinas with the archives and six thousand cartridges. The only foreign capture of the California capital in the Spanish period; Monterey was taken again by Commodore Jones in 1842 and by Commodore Sloat in 1846.
properties.result: Monterey falls; the only foreign capture of the capital under Spanish rule

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 220-49.

properties.name: Bouchard at Refugio
properties.summary: Bouchard's men landed at Refugio, plundered the Ortega rancho and killed cattle, and sailed again the next morning. Three of the party were taken in an ambush: Lieutenant William Taylor of Boston, Martin Romero of Paraguay, and Mateo Jose Pascual. Bancroft twice says probably of the dates; the ships were off Santa Barbara on the 6th.
properties.result: Ranch plundered; 3 captured by Spanish ambush

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 236-37.

properties.name: Bouchard at Santa Barbara · Guerra's Bluff
properties.summary: Bouchard anchors. Guerra bluffs with marching troops trick; soldiers march around a hill repeatedly to look like a large army. Prisoner exchange. No fighting.
properties.result: Bluff succeeds; no attack

sources.citation: Bancroft II:237–239.

properties.name: Bouchard at San Juan Capistrano
properties.summary: Bouchard lands. Minor damage; straw houses burned, wine spilled. 4 insurgent deserters surrender.
properties.result: Minor damage

sources.citation: Bancroft II:240–241.

properties.name: La Pérouse at Monterey
properties.summary: The first foreign account of Spanish military capacity in California, and of the size of the Spanish claim. La Perouse reports the claim at second hand and does not stop it at Mount St Elias; he says it has no stopping place at all: 'North California, the most northern settlement in which is Saint Francis, in latitude 37 deg. 58', has, according to the opinion of the governor of Monterey, no other boundary than that of America; and our ships, in penetrating as far as Mount Saint Elias, have not reached its limits.' Against that he sets what he counted: a government more than eight hundred leagues in circumference whose governor's 'real subjects consist only of two hundred and eighty-two cavalry', garrisoning five small forts and finding detachments of four or five men for each of twenty-five missions, to restrain 'about fifty thousand wandering Indians', of whom nearly ten thousand had been baptized. A continental claim against that, seven years before Nootka.
properties.result: France prints the claim and the garrison roll on facing pages

sources.citation: La Perouse, A Voyage Round the World, performed in the years 1785, 1786, 1787 and 1788, ed. Milet-Mureau, English translation (London: Johnson, 1799), ii. 196 (the garrison) and ii. 224-25 (the boundary); French original, Voyage de La Perouse autour du monde (Paris, 1797).

properties.name: Coast Miwok Intelligence to Sal
properties.summary: Coast Miwok informant tells Commandant Sal two ships at Bodega; soldiers "dressed like ours turned inside out." Earliest warning of foreign presence, 3 weeks before diplomatic intelligence through official channels.
properties.result: Indigenous networks faster than imperial intelligence

properties.name: Coast Miwok Deceive Goycoechea
properties.summary: The Coast Miwok told Goycoechea, through his interpreter, that there was a vessel at the mouth of the port and that if he went their way he could speak to its captain, 'as the lagoon joined the sea and we could not cross it'. He went that way, down the west side of Tomales Bay, against instructions that had ordered him up the east side, and found he could not get round. Meeting Matute on 8 August he consulted him 'about the deceit practiced on me by the natives who had assured me that I could not cross the lagoon because it made a turn and entered the sea'. Wagner, editing him, suggests he may simply have misunderstood them. Either way, what the Spanish party did with its horses that week was settled by what the people of the lagoon told it.
properties.result: A Spanish march routed by local information, mistaken or given

sources.citation: Goycoechea's diary, 6 to 8 August 1793, AGN Seccion Historia vol. 70, translated in Wagner, CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 342-44, with the editor's notes 69 and 73.

properties.name: Coast Miwok Calibrated Diplomacy at Tomales Bay
properties.summary: Ten or twelve leagues along the inlet on 7 August, Goycoechea counted nine settlements. The Indians travelling with him said these were 'prepared to give us battle'; he passed all of them 'without noticing any of the inhabitants in any warlike demonstration', and 'instead, they presented my men with pinole and some little fruits from the beach', which he repaid in beads and food. Note whose assessment the warning was: it came from his own companions, not from the villages. What the villages did was decide, nine times over, how to meet an armed party on their shore.
properties.result: Capability held in reserve; nine villages choosing the same way

sources.citation: Goycoechea's diary, 7 August 1793, AGN Seccion Historia vol. 70, translated in Wagner, CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 343.

properties.name: Coast Miwok Bilingual Intermediaries at Bodega
properties.summary: The same party Menzies met on 20 October 1793: one man, five women and some children, who called out 'Amico' and spoke many words of Spanish, and who pointed repeatedly up the lagoon when they said the word for Spaniards. Wagner reads that pointing as evidence that Matute's establishment stood further up the water. People with a working command of one empire's language, giving a second empire directions to the first.
properties.result: Brokers between two empires, with the language of one of them

sources.citation: Menzies' California journal, CHSQ 2, no. 4 (1924), 302-03.
Wagner, CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 338, on the pointing up the lagoon.

properties.name: Guirmenes Intel on Bodega · "Keep This Indian Happy"
properties.summary: Indigenous informant (Guirmenes) reports no foreign ship at Bodega for 2 years. Governor orders: "previene se tenga á ese indio contento" (keep this Indian happy). Indigenous surveillance network sustained across years; Spain depends on it.
properties.result: Spain pays for indigenous intelligence

properties.name: Suisun Resist Moraga at Carquinez
properties.summary: Suisun warriors fight Moraga at the Strait. Had killed 16 Christians over prior 3 years. This is a military frontier; Spain fights across it, does not govern beyond it.
properties.result: Indigenous military control of the Strait frontier

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 91 and n. 24, citing Arrillaga's report at Prov. Rec. ix. 122-23 (C-A 25); Vallejo, Recuerdos, Tomo 1 ch. 10, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 151-52.

properties.name: Suispaques Evade Cabo Ortega
properties.summary: Cabo Ortega dispatched to capture Suispaques/Guispaques; returned without success. Indigenous captain later offered to return fugitives himself; on his own terms.
properties.result: Indigenous autonomy; Spanish military cannot operate here

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. p. 63 / Savage p. 16 / scan n15, Doc 53. Arrillaga, Soledad, 2 October 1811, approving the despatch of Cabo Juan Ortega in pursuit of the gentiles of the rancheria of Suispaques.
Prov. Rec. (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 64-66 / Savage p. 17 / scan n16, Doc 56. Arrillaga, Soledad, 31 October 1811: Cabo Ortega returned without having taken the gentile Suispaques.

properties.name: Chief Vallí-éla Requests Russian Flag
properties.summary: Chief Vallí-éla of Bodega Miwok requests Russian protection and asks Golovnin for a Russian flag. "Very glad to have Russian neighbors." Three independent accounts (Golovnin, Matiushkin, Lütke). The indigenous chief chooses his empire.
properties.result: Indigenous imperial choice; requests Russian protection

sources.citation: Golovnin, Around the World on the Kamchatka, 1817-1819, trans. Wiswell (1979), 165, cited in Farris, 'The Russian Imprint on the Colonization of California' (1998), 6.
Archive of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire (AVPRI), the Golovnin materials.

properties.name: Gualinela's Armed Resistance · 200 Men
properties.summary: Chief Gualinela of Tiutume ranchería (Bodega), 43 people. 200 armed men; heathen + Christian neophytes from Mission San Rafael; band together to resist Mexican troops. Cross-mission alliance.
properties.result: Armed indigenous coalition; 40 years of continuity at Bodega

sources.citation: Farris 1998:7 (Vallejo report).

properties.name: Sal's Boundary Letter · "English Want SF Bay for a Boundary"
properties.summary: Sal to Arrillaga, reporting the intelligence Bodega y Quadra brought back from Nootka: «Segun sus espresiones, quieren los ingleses la boca de este puerto por línea divisoria», by their own account the English want the mouth of this port for the dividing line. The same letter reports a burst cannon and two English frigates at Bodega.
properties.result: The boundary claim stated explicitly

sources.citation: St. Pap., Sac. (BANC MSS C-A 54), tomo i, orig. pp. 657-8 / Savage p. 120 / scan n119, Doc 279. Bancroft cites this leaf as St. Pap., Sac., MS., i. 119.

properties.name: SF Cannon Burst · Sole Weapon Destroyed
properties.summary: Cannon exploded during saint's day firing. 10 pieces, fragments reached church 125 varas. Fired by Soldado Arriola. San Francisco's sole defensive weapon destroyed before the Nootka crisis peaked.
properties.result: One cannon, and it burst

properties.name: Arrillaga: "Presidios Are Indefensible · English Said So"
properties.summary: "Los Presidios de Alta Cal. están indefensos, cuya circunstancia ha sido notada por los mismos ingleses... no pueden resistir contra una invasion." The governor's own admission to his viceroy.
properties.result: Spain admits its own weakness

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 14), tomo xxi, orig. pp. 236-237 / Savage p. 94 / scan n93. Arrillaga to the Viceroy, San Diego, 16 March 1793: «Representa q.e los Presidios de Alta Cal. estan indefensos, cuya circunstancia ha sido notada p.r los mismos ingleses». The same entry reports eight English prisoners at Monterey.

properties.name: Arrillaga: "Tierra Incognita"
properties.summary: «El grande rodeo y tierra incognita». Asked to open a road from San Francisco to Bodega, the governor reported the overland route impossible: the great detour, and unknown country. The ground in question begins about forty-five miles north of the presidio he was writing from.
properties.result: The governor reports the country north of the Gate as unknown

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 14), tomo xxii, orig. p. ~290 / scan n112, Doc 99. Arrillaga, 1793. Bancroft's shelfmark xxi. 113 belongs to a different despatch of 20 August 1793.

properties.name: Viceroy Orders Bodega · "Whether or Not English Are There"
properties.summary: Revilla Gigedo ordered Bodega reconnoitred and occupied, to deny foreigners a shelter next door to the presidios, together with a fortification plan for Bodega, San Francisco, Monterey and San Diego. None of it was built. Sal reallocated the Bodega stores to San Francisco the following summer.
properties.result: Order given; never carried out

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 22), tomo ii, orig. pp. 144-148.
Bancroft, History of California I, 506-08, citing Prov. St. Pap., MS., xi. 92 for the viceroy's order of 6 July 1793.

properties.name: Fiscal: "Fortifications Would Not Prevent a Landing"
properties.summary: Crown fiscal officer declares defense should be naval; land fortifications useless. Devastating assessment from within the imperial bureaucracy itself.
properties.result: Spain's own bureaucracy declares California indefensible

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 8), tomo xv, orig. pp. 764-765 / Savage p. 443 / leaf 247 / scan n444. Branciforte to the Governor of California, Orizaba, 22 May 1797, on the receipt of Cordoba's plans of San Diego and the Santa Barbara channel: the Fiscal de Real Hacienda holds that «la defensa de aquellos establecimientos debe hacerse por la marina», at less cost than works that «no embarazarian el desembarco».

properties.name: Yerba Buena Battery Abandoned
properties.summary: Argüello reports Yerba Buena Battery unmanned; only a daily visit by the vigía. SF garrison: 1 cabo, 4 artilleros, 3 cabos, 10 soldados. Barely sufficient for Presidio + fort. The key battery controlling the narrows has no one in it.
properties.result: Key battery unmanned; "imaginary" defense

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), tomo xviii, orig. pp. 80-81. Arguello on the garrison left at San Francisco, one corporal, four artillerymen, three corporals and ten volunteer soldiers, barely enough for the guards of the presidio and the fort, «quedando abandonada la Bateria de Yerba Buena», visited daily by the lookout and every eight days by the artillery corporal.

properties.name: Pedro de Nava: Isolation Was Deliberate Policy
properties.summary: Comandante General of the Provincias Internas explicitly rejects overland California–New Mexico road. Cites 1786 prohibition. California's territories "useless." Indigenous nations form impassable barrier. The only route is the Sea of Cortez.
properties.result: Isolation was policy, not accident

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), tomo xviii, orig. pp. 101-103. Pedro de Nava, Comandante General de las Provincias Internas, to the Viceroy, Chihuahua, 20 July 1800, on the project of a road between California and New Mexico and a presidio on the Colorado: he argues against both, and against extending the presidio line, as «abasando inutilmente inmensos territorios que de mucho tiempo de nada nos pueden servir». Savage's copy.
Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 11), tomo xviii, orig. pp. 101-103 (continued). El Fiscal de lo Civil, Mexico, 4 March 1801, his parecer on the same project.

properties.name: Fortress San Joaquín in Collapse
properties.summary: Manuel Gomez's report on the fort: eight cannons, two of them unserviceable, the twelve-pounder's mounting bad and its bore pitted, the eight-pounder's ball jamming for want of a rasador; the gunner's tools broken; two cannons at the landing place unusable for want of platform planking and emplaced in sand; and not a single veteran artilleryman fit for duty. Two years after Bouchard had proved the place could be taken, and still not repaired.
properties.result: The fortress is a ruin

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. i.1110-1113 / Savage pp. 261-263 / scan n260-n262, Doc 332. Manuel Gomez to Gov. Sola, San Francisco, 20 March 1820.

properties.name: Solá to the Viceroy: San Rafael and the Russians in One Despatch
properties.summary: One despatch carries both the new establishment at San Rafael and the warning about the Russian posts at Ross and Bodega. That the two concerns travelled together is the fact; that the mission was founded for the Russians is a further claim the letter does not settle. Bancroft, reading the same April 1818 report, gives the health of the San Francisco neophytes as doubtless the true reason for the foundation, and attributes the anti-Russian motive to Russian writers rather than to the Spanish record.
properties.result: Two concerns in one despatch; the motive is contested, not proved

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. pp. 583-604 / scan n429-n449, Doc 756: Sola's report to the Viceroy, Monterey, 3 April 1818, on the Russian establishments at Ross and Bodega.
Bancroft, History of California II, 328-29, 372, for the health reason and the Russian-writers attribution.

properties.name: The 1793 Bodega Occupation Attempt
properties.summary: The occupation the whole story turns on. Alarmed that Colnett's 1790 stay at Bodega would draw other Britons to take possession, the viceroy ordered the port occupied. Juan Bautista Matute went ahead in the schooner Sutil about 1 April 1793 to put up buildings; later that month the Aranzazu, under Salvador Melendez Valdes, followed with the garrison and the artisans to form a regular establishment. The Aranzazu reached Bodega on 16 July and had to anchor five or six leagues from the site, which Matute judged she could not enter, so he landed the troops, artisans, food and supplies at San Francisco instead. He had already run up some kind of barracks near the south end of the sand dunes, two miles from the end of Bodega Head, and Goycoechea saw them standing on 11 August. Matute was back at San Francisco by 12 August; five days later Arrillaga told the viceroy that the occupation of Bodega was put off for that year. The postponement turned out to be permanent, and the ten soldiers and five mechanics with the Bodega stores stayed at San Francisco under Sal. Matute gave the reason as a want of timber for building.
properties.result: The establishment that did not happen; Spain's claim north of the Gate never occupied

sources.citation: Matute's report to the provisional commandant of the department of San Blas, San Blas, 7 November 1793, translated in Wagner, 'The Last Spanish Exploration of the Northwest Coast', California Historical Society Quarterly 10, no. 4 (1931), 338, 340-46.

Bancroft, History of California I, 507-08, on the Aranzazu's arrival at San Francisco on 24 July, Goycoechea's departure on 5 August, Matute's return on 12 August, Arrillaga's postponement, and the ten soldiers and five mechanics retained by Sal.

Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 14), tomo xxii, orig. p. ~273-4 / Savage p. 107 / scan n106, Doc 468. Arrillaga to the Viceroy, Monterey, 16 July 1793, acknowledging the order that the port of Bodega be occupied.
St. Pap., Missions (C-A 15), Doc 515: the presidios and Bodega, 16 July 1793.

properties.name: Bodega Establishment Abandoned
properties.summary: Sal reports that the establishment at the port of Bodega will not be carried out, and that the articles destined for it have been reassigned to the San Francisco presidio. The words are Savage's digest of the letter rather than Sal's own, and the entry records no act of abandonment: what it records is Sal disposing of the Bodega stores on his own understanding that nothing further was coming. The closing bracket on the 1793 order and attempt.
properties.result: Supplies redirected to San Francisco; nothing further ordered for Bodega

sources.citation: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 15), Doc 520: Sal to Arrillaga, 25 July 1794. Savage's abstract, which expands the manuscript's establecim.to.

properties.name: Wilcocks Calls at Russian Bodega · and the Annexation Plot
properties.summary: The American trader James Smith Wilcocks calls at "un establecimiento ruso llamado Bodega"; "los rusos no quisieron comprar nada"; then sells Gov. Solá $700 of blankets for the four presidios. In 1817 he is accused of plotting to "levantarme con las Californias para integrarlas a los anglo-americanos"; the earliest dated articulation of the U.S.-annexation fear the open coast invited.
properties.result: Bodega as a (failed) commercial port in the US–Russian–Spanish triangle

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. i.716-726 / Savage pp. 166-172 / scan n165-n171, Doc 206. Wilcocks's «historia exacta», Guaymas, 1817: left Hawaii 7 October and reached «un establecimiento ruso llamado Bodega» on the 25th [October 1816], but «los rusos no quisieron comprar nada»; then Santa Barbara, and at Monterey sold Gov. Sola $700 of manta for the four presidios.

Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), orig. pp. i.~716 / Savage pp. 163-165 / scan n162-n164, Doc 203. Wilcocks to Gov. Sola, Guaymas, 12 December 1817, denouncing the slander that he meant «levantarme con las Californias para integrarlas a los anglo-americanos mis paisanos».

properties.name: Elliot de Castro / Ilmena Seized at Refugio
properties.summary: The Russian brig Ilmena's shore party; John Elliot de Castro, an American, an Aleut and others; is seized at Ortega's Refugio rancho, the coast's otter-smuggling rendezvous. A $2,000 ransom is offered and refused. Spain/Mexico can catch the people but not stop the trade.
properties.result: The Mexican-era sequel; Refugio as a second Bodega-style keyhole

properties.name: RAC Parlamentario · Podushkin on the Chirikoff at Monterey
properties.summary: Baranov, from Novo-Arkhangelsk, protests 'insults to the Russian Flag and the capture and keeping in cruel bondage of Russians and other people subject to our august Monarch in the waters and coasts of California', invokes articles 3 and 4 of the treaty of 1812, says he has petitioned the Emperor, and sends Lieutenant Yakov Podushkin aboard the Chirikoff as a parlamentario. The English is Ivan Petroff's, made for the Bancroft project seventy years later, not Baranov's own and not a 1817 translation; Petroff's reliability as a translator for Bancroft is a standing problem. Podushkin's own errand at Monterey was narrower: the arrest and return of a Kodiak sailor, Peter Leonoff, who had deserted the Chirikoff at Little Bodega on 30 March.
properties.result: Russia treats with Spain as a power on the California coast

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. i.866-870 / Savage pp. 207-209 / scan n206-n208, Doc 264. Baranov to Gov. Sola, Novo-Arkhangelsk, 2 February 1817, in Ivan Petroff's English translation; leaf verified.
Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), orig. p. i.868 / Savage p. 206 / scan n205, Doc 263. Lt. Yakov Podushkin to Gov. Sola, Monterey, aboard the Chirikoff, 22 April 1817.

properties.name: Kuskov's RAC Letters to the SF Commandant
properties.summary: Ivan Kuskov, RAC commercial councillor at Ross, writes directly to the SF commandant "in the name of the Honorable Russian-American Company under special protection of His Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias," sending agent Slobodchikov to settle accounts and pressing for the return of captured Kodiak Aleuts.
properties.result: Ross corresponds with SF as one sovereign to another

properties.name: Spanish Missions Supply Kuskov at Fort Ross
properties.summary: The Spanish missions supplying Kuskov's Russian colony; Spain's own establishments provisioning the foreign outpost on the ground it claimed. The open coast as routine economic fact, running in Spain's disfavor.
properties.result: Spain provisions the colony it was ordered to uproot

properties.name: Fort Ross Abandonment Resolved
properties.summary: The RAC Main Board resolves to abandon Ross and "sell or barter for wheat to the inhabitants of San Francisco." The otter gone, Ross is liquidated; the economic close of the arc that opened with the resource.
properties.result: Russia leaves; Ross sold to Sutter, a promoter of the US invasion

sources.citation: Fort Ross AVPRI, 1841 abandonment resolution (via Gibson & Istomin).

properties.name: Yanovsky's RAC Trade Overture
properties.summary: RAC chief manager Semyon Yanovsky proposes a joint, equal-shares otter-hunt and open commerce (via Khlebnikov and the Madrid embassy; the Ilmena to supply Ross). Solá replies he cannot grant otter-hunting; only the Viceroy can. The third volume of one continuous Russo-Spanish negotiation.
properties.result: Russia again negotiates as a commercial sovereign; Spain defers to Mexico City

sources.citation: C-A 55 Docs 333–334 (Yanovsky / Solá, ~1820).

properties.name: The Suvorov at SF + the RAC Proclamation to California
properties.summary: The RAC ship Suvorov (Lazarev) calls at San Francisco carrying a formal RAC directors' overture "to the noble and honoured Spanish inhabitants of California," invoking Russo-Spanish friendship, the 1812 treaty, and Rezanov's 1806 visit; the institutional Russian demand for the California provision trade, arriving by ship.
properties.result: The RAC's formal trade-opening request, delivered to SF

sources.citation: C-A 12 C478 + C479 (Suvorov 1815; passport-proclamation St. Petersburg, 12 Jul 1811).

properties.name: British Squadron Sounds San Diego Harbor
properties.summary: A sworn deposition of 28 June 1799: a British naval squadron waiting for the Manila galleon, with twenty-two prizes taken off Peru, meant to winter at San Diego, whose harbour its boats had already sounded in secret one moonlit night a year or two before, working «instruidos por los planos de Nutka». The English phrasing above is the cataloguer's rendering of the Spanish, not the document's own words; the deponent's name for the officer concerned is read doubtfully in the manuscript. The open coast as a reconnaissance ground, which is exactly what the 1793 order had feared.
properties.result: San Diego's harbor already mapped by the enemy; the threat the 1793 order feared

sources.citation: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 15), Doc 392: deposition taken at Loreto, 28 June 1799.

properties.name: Presidio of San Francisco
properties.summary: 1776. Northernmost military post. $1,400 total investment by 1793. Garrison: ~35 men.

properties.name: Fort San Joaquín (Castillo de SF)
properties.summary: 1794. Battery guarding the Golden Gate narrows. 1 cannon (burst 1792), 8 by 1793, 6 functional by 1820. Unmanned by 1800.

properties.name: Presidio of Monterey
properties.summary: 1770. Capital of Alta California. Burned by Bouchard 1818.

properties.name: Presidio of San Diego
properties.summary: 1769. First presidio. Punta de Guijarros battery.

properties.name: Mission San José
properties.summary: 1797. Staging base for Central Valley expeditions.

properties.name: Mission San Rafael
properties.summary: Founded December 1817 as a branch of San Francisco, 83 days after the Hagemeister agreement, and without a boat of its own. Whether it was meant as a counterweight to Ross is contested: Bancroft gives the health of the San Francisco neophytes as the reason and credits the anti-Russian reading to Russian writers.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 328-29.

properties.name: Mission San Francisco Solano (Sonoma)
properties.summary: Founded 1823, the northernmost of the missions. The sentence often attached to its founding, that at the moment Spain acknowledged Mexican independence the friars would all be Russians, is not Altimira's: Bancroft prints it as the declaration in a letter sent from Mexico to one of the friars, which Padre Duran recapitulated in January 1823 along with Iturbide's remark that the Russians were threatening Mexico in the Californias.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 483.

properties.name: Pueblo de San José
properties.summary: 1777. First civilian settlement in Alta California.

properties.name: Villa de Branciforte (Santa Cruz)
properties.summary: 1797. Third and last pueblo. Named for Viceroy Branciforte. Planned as strategic settlement near Santa Cruz mission.

properties.name: Santa Eulalia (Cordelia)
properties.summary: ~1824. Mission Solano farming outpost; house for padre, corral, neophyte in charge. Suisun Valley.

properties.name: Port Rumiantsev (Bodega Bay)
properties.summary: ~1807. RAC fur-collecting base. First representative: Tarakanov. Permanent.
properties.notes: Anchorage in Bodega Harbor; the precise landing/port site is approximate.

properties.name: Fort Ross (Metini)
properties.summary: 1812. Ivan Kuskov. 95 Russians, ~80 Aleut. 12 guns, 3 falconets. No Spanish opposition.

properties.name: Farallon Islands Sealing Station
properties.summary: From about 1812. Some 29 miles west of the Golden Gate. Seasonal Aleut camps for the Ross settlement. Never contested.

properties.name: Kostromitinov Ranch
properties.summary: 1833. Russian River near Willow Creek. ~100 acres wheat by 1841.
properties.notes: Exact ranch site debated (Osborn); descriptions place it on the south side of the Russian River near its mouth.

properties.name: Khlebnikov Ranch
properties.summary: 1833. Upper Salmon Creek valley, ~5 mi E of Bodega. Largest ranch; bakery, forge, tobacco shed.

properties.name: Chernykh Ranch
properties.summary: ~1833. Near Graton (Purrington Creek). First vineyard in Sonoma County.

properties.name: The Sonora Names Puerto de la Bodega
properties.summary: Returning from the north, Bodega y Quadra's 36-foot schooner Sonora anchors and names the Puerto de la Bodega, charting it with keyed points and soundings; the founding document of the Spanish claim to this coast. Which water he actually anchored in is a live scholarly dispute: Edwards (1964) demonstrates the 1775 anchorage was Tomales Bay and the name later migrated north; Wagner (1926) read the chart as Bodega Harbor.
properties.result: The port named and claimed

sources.citation: Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms: El Puerto de la Bodega and Bodega Bay', Pacific Historical Review 33 (1964)
Plano del Puerto de la Bodega (1775), Savage copy in C-A 15
Wagner, Sir Francis Drake's Voyage Around the World (1926), 158–59 (the Bodega-Harbor reading)

properties.notes: Drawn at Bodega Harbor for continuity with the migrated name; see the companion conjectural point for the Tomales reading.

properties.name: The 1775 Anchorage · the Tomales Reading
properties.summary: Edwards's reconstruction: the water the Sonora entered on 3 October 1775, the original Puerto de la Bodega, was Tomales Bay, and everything called Bodega on the modern map carries a migrated name. Against it stands what the Spanish themselves told Vancouver's people in 1793. Menzies records that the San Diego commandant's plan of the coast showed both waters, and that the Spanish called the lagoon the Chatham's boat had visited, the one behind Bodega Head, Port Bodega, while 'the other to the Southward of it which goes to the South East they calld Port Juan Francisco'. Goycoechea's diary of August 1793 uses the two names the same way. The identification is genuinely open, but in 1793 the northern water already carried the name.
properties.result: Identification debated; the 1793 Spanish usage runs against the Tomales reading

sources.citation: Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms: El Puerto de la Bodega and Bodega Bay', Pacific Historical Review 33 (1964).
Menzies' California journal, CHSQ 2, no. 4 (1924), 335, for the Spanish names on the commandant's plan.
Goycoechea's diary, 6 to 13 August 1793, AGN Seccion Historia vol. 70, translated in Wagner, CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 342-45.

properties.notes: Drawn hollow: a scholarly reconstruction, not a documented position.

properties.name: Matute on the Sutil: the Occupation Given Up
properties.summary: Juan Bautista Matute came up in the schooner Sutil about 1 April 1793 to put up the buildings for the Bodega settlement, found no English, and gave the occupation up: the Aranzazu could not be brought in, there was no timber for building, and the Sutil alone was not enough. He had got some kind of barracks up near the south end of the sand dunes, two miles from the end of Bodega Head, which Goycoechea saw on 11 August. Two ships left Bodega together the day before Goycoechea arrived on the 10th; Matute was at San Francisco by the 12th, stayed until 10 October, and reached San Blas on 7 November, where he wrote his report. His people did not go with him: he landed the troops, artisans, food and supplies at San Francisco, left the food and the troops there in service, and brought four artisans back to San Blas. Bancroft has ten soldiers and five mechanics retained by Sal with the Bodega stores. If Edwards is right about the 1775 name, Matute was also surveying a different water from the one Bodega had praised.
properties.result: Occupation given up; the garrison absorbed into San Francisco

sources.citation: Matute's report, San Blas, 7 November 1793, translated in Wagner, CHSQ 10, no. 4 (1931), 340-46; Wagner's account at 338.
Bancroft, History of California I, 507-08.
Matute's resultas of the Bodega commission (AGN, Historia 71).
Matute's 1793 plan of Bodega (AHN, Estado, MPD. 33).
Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964), for the wrong-harbour argument.

properties.name: San Francisco · 'the Last Point We Can Hold'
properties.summary: A long fiscal report on the Californias defines New California as running from San Diego to San Francisco inclusive; the last point Spain can hold in full and independent dominion on this coast under the Nootka convention. The empire's own paperwork drew its ceiling at the Golden Gate before the Russians ever landed.

quote.es: …hasta el de San Francisco inclusive, como último punto que podemos poseer con completo é independiente dominio en la costa del Sur…
quote.en: …to San Francisco inclusive, as the last point we can possess in complete and independent dominion on the southern coast…

sources.citation: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 54), doc 216

properties.name: Vancouver's Open-Door Claim
properties.summary: In the Nootka negotiation Vancouver claims for Britain free access to Spanish establishments made or to be made; 'que se hayan hecho, ó se hagan'; as far south as San Francisco. The claim, delivered in a Spanish translation Bodega y Quadra could read unaided, declared this coast's door open two decades before Ross was built.

quote.es: …los establecimientos que se hayan hecho, ó se hagan…
quote.en: …the establishments that have been made, or shall be made…

sources.citation: Vancouver–Bodega correspondence, Nootka 1792 (AHN, Estado, leg. 4290, exp. 1)

properties.notes: Anchored at San Francisco, the claim's named southern limit.

properties.name: Calleja's Precautions · the Russians at Bodega
properties.summary: Viceroy Calleja writes the governor on the Russian establishment at Bodega, ordering precautions against Americans and against privateers: Mexico City registering, in the middle of the insurgency, that the coast north of the Gate now answered to somebody else's initiative. The same despatch carries the Baja California parallel.

sources.citation: Provincial State Papers (C-A 12), doc 491 · Calleja to the Gov. of California, 9 Jul 1813

properties.name: San Rafael Attacked · the Piña Expedition
properties.summary: Mission San Rafael, its long-serving padre Juan Amoros dead that year and its population falling, is attacked by gentiles, and an expedition goes out under Lazaro Pina. Amoros was not the founder: Luis Gil y Taboada took charge of the branch establishment at the 1817 founding, and Amoros served there until his death. Word of the rising travelled through fugitive mission Indians to the rancherias around Ross, and is the likely referent of the Russian report of a San Rafael revolt in the spring of 1832.
properties.result: The North Bay crisis opens

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California III, 716 (citing Vallejo, Documentos, MS, i. 307) for the attack and the Pina expedition; III, 719, and II, 328-29, for Gil y Taboada at the founding and Amoros's death in 1832.
Bolkhovitinov and Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6, for the Russian report.

properties.name: The Mercado Affair
properties.summary: Padre Mercado of San Rafael, claiming he feared an attack to free the visitors he had already seized, sent his majordomo Molina out on the morning of 20 May with thirty-seven armed neophytes. They surprised the strangers, killed twenty-one, wounded many more and took twenty men, women and children prisoner, against five wounded of their own, one mortally. Mercado reported it coolly to Figueroa five days later and asked for reinforcements. Figueroa, indignant that his promises to the Indians had been violated, sent the case to Prefect Garcia Diego as the competent ecclesiastical judge, and it was the prefect who suspended Mercado from his ministry and summoned him to Santa Clara. Vallejo, on Figueroa's orders, freed the prisoners at San Francisco and San Rafael and toured the rancherias to calm them. Mercado was out of arrest by the middle of the following year.
properties.result: Figueroa refers the case; the prefect suspends the padre

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California III, 322-24, summarised at III, 716.

properties.name: Kashaya Resistance at Ross
properties.summary: With the otter gone and Ross living off its grain, manager Kostromitinov's parties seize Kashaya laborers by force; Wrangell records up to 150 gathered, families 'driven to the settlement like cattle to work'. Kashaya and Miwok answer with five years of attacks on company property, culminating in an 1838 raid that kills about a hundred Ross cattle. Indian resistance becomes one cause of the colony's unprofitability and sale.
properties.result: Resistance presses on the colony's economics

sources.citation: Wrangell and Kostromitonov, ethnographic reports (Stross trans., 1974)
Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6

properties.name: RAC Possession Plate No. 14 · Malaya Bodega
properties.summary: Kuskov's expedition buries numbered metal claiming plate No. 14 at 'Malaya Bodega,' the inner harbor; one of a chain of iron plates with brass crosses by which the company staked New Albion years before Ross was built (No. 1 at Trinidad, 1808).
properties.result: The coast staked in metal

sources.citation: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12)
Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

properties.name: RAC Possession Plate No. 20 · Drake's Estero
properties.summary: A second numbered claiming plate buried at the mouth of Drake's Estero; the company quietly marking the shore of New Albion down to 38°.

sources.citation: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12)
Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

properties.name: The Buried Eagle · a Plate in San Pablo Bay
properties.summary: The company later reported placing 'plate No. 1000 and one coat of arms'; a double-headed eagle; at 'Malaya Bodega, in the northern arm of San Francisco, where the fort and mission of the Spaniards were built': a possession marker buried inside the Spanish bay itself, in the waters of San Pablo Bay. Its spot has never been found.
properties.result: A claim buried inside Spanish waters

sources.citation: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12)
Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

properties.notes: Position conjectural; drawn hollow; the RAC report's geography is ambiguous.
